evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: oracle-bone component analysis and early use
evidence.text: The database interprets oracle-bone and bronze 東 as a filled sack tied at both ends, with “bag” as the graphic sense, and reports early directional use, including oracle-bone 合集9735「東土受年」 and Western Zhou bronze examples. These are the database’s paleographic and usage analyses; its reported inscription citations were not independently inspected as artifacts here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析（東）

evidence.source: 陳雅雯, 成大中文學報 27
evidence.text: The article argues that a sack as the original referent is debatable because many early 東 contexts are names or ritual terms rather than attested sack uses. It also questions whether sound resemblance alone explains borrowing and discusses the possibility that early graph forms relate to 日 and 木 and that the Shuowen account preserves cultural tradition. This is a counteranalysis, not a settled alternative proof.
evidence.title: 說「東」

evidence.field: 東, 束 and 橐 graph and sound analyses
evidence.text: The article treats 東 and 束 forms as closely related and reports them interchangeable in bronze inscriptions; it proposes the 東 bag image was borrowed by sound to write “east.” It gives Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese 東 *tˤoŋ and 束 *s-tʰok, while describing 橐 *tʰˤak in its separate discussion of 石 as a sound component in 橐. These reconstructed forms do not independently establish the spoken name of the depicted bag, so the whole-graph loan’s source-name match remains unverified.
evidence.title: Explaining the Directions 東西南北, part 1: 東西

evidence.field: 東 entry and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The entry gives the Eastern Han dictionary’s account「東，動也。从木。官溥說：从日在木中」. The online transcription also gives Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary linking 木 to 榑木 and comparing 東 with 杲 and 杳. This is a historical graphic interpretation, not direct evidence of the oracle-bone graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「東」

evidence.text: Records Standard Mandarin dōng (Hanyu Pinyin), Guangzhou–Hong Kong Cantonese dung1 (Jyutping), Middle Chinese Baxter tuwng, Guangyun 德紅切, Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *tˤoŋ (with an uncertainty note) and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *toːŋ. These are separate transcription or reconstruction systems, not one interchangeable pronunciation.
evidence.title: 東 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, University of Michigan project
evidence.text: The project page identifies its downloadable reconstructions as supplementary material to Baxter and Sagart’s 2014 Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction. The entry-level 東 and 束 values cited above were presented in Outlier’s discussion, not independently confirmed from a specific item in the project downloads in this inspection.
evidence.title: The Baxter-Sagart reconstruction of Old Chinese

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: oracle-bone, bronze and later graphic interpretation
evidence.text: The database rejects the Shuowen 日-in-木 analysis as the explanation of the early graph while presenting early forms and a sack interpretation. The dossier and the examined source do not establish a complete, specimen-by-specimen transition sequence or show that every early form represents the same pictured object.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析（東）

evidence.text: The received poem text has「嘒彼小星，三五在東」, a literary directional use. The page identifies a received text tradition, not the composition date or earliest surviving physical witness. An attempt to open the page returned 403; the search result displayed the text.
evidence.title: Book of Poetry: Lessons from the states: Odes of Shao and the South: Xiao Xing

evidence.field: oracle-script glyph candidate, description, provenance and rights
evidence.text: File description identifies a vector redraw of 東 in oracle-script style and names source databases including Xiaoxuetang, hanziyuan, CUHK and Chinese Text Project; it also cites hanziyuan image J14291. The file is a modern Inkscape-created representation, not a photograph of an oracle-bone artifact. Its file page declares the SVG representation public domain.
evidence.title: File:東-oracle.svg

evidence.field: Shang bronze glyph candidate, description, source and rights
evidence.text: File description identifies a vector redraw in Shang bronze script style and cites 東父乙尊 (late Shang) as the source note. It names Xiaoxuetang, hanziyuan, CUHK, Chinese Text Project and Chinese Linguipedia as available sources. The SVG was created in Inkscape and the file page declares the representation public domain; it is not a photograph of the vessel inscription.
evidence.title: File:東-bronze-shang.svg

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The guide says its ancient-form resources include oracle-bone, bronze and Warring States manuscript materials, and that entries may draw on published paleographic works and collections. It distinguishes early graph form and historical word usage, supporting use of its records as a scholarly database account rather than treating each displayed glyph as an artifact photograph.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫使用凡例

evidence.field: rights notice for query-interface glyph images
evidence.text: The official license notice states that glyph images and glyph-attribute information obtained through the database query interface are released under CC0 1.0. The inspected 東 record page did not expose a direct image URL in its accessible text, so no Xiaoxuetang image is proposed here.
evidence.title: 小學堂版權聲明

evidence.text: The page lists Đông’s senses including east and host, and states that all rights are reserved. It is linked here only as evidence; its glyph is not selected as an image asset.
evidence.title: 漢字「東」：基本資料

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, dictionary page surfaced in search
evidence.field: 東家 example and landlord meaning
evidence.text: Search result for the dictionary entry includes a Du Fu quotation using 東家, supporting a Tang-era literary example for the host/household sense. The associated page open attempt returned 403, so the text was not independently inspected beyond the search result.
evidence.title: 東家 - Chinese Text Project dictionary

evidence.text: The dictionary records the east direction, host/owner, spring and toilet senses, and cites the Shuowen account and a Tang Du Fu 東家 example. It does not establish first dates or secure semantic links for all listed senses; the gloss list is not used as a chronology.
evidence.title: 東 dōng - 汉典

evidence.text: File description identifies an Inkscape vector redraw of 東 in Shuowen seal-script style, traces the represented graph to source databases including Xiaoxuetang and cites a hanziyuan image. The file page declares the representation public domain. It is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact photograph.
evidence.title: File:東-seal.svg

gaps: The proposed early bag/sack picture is a significant paleographic analysis but remains disputed; NCKU’s article argues that the earliest contexts do not attest a sack sense and that phonology alone does not fully explain why this graph was chosen for east.

A whole-graph loan from the depicted object's name is not independently established: no source inspected recovers the object's ancient spoken name and pronunciation. Reconstructions for 東 alone cannot establish the name of the pictured sack, so the proposed sound match remains uncertain.
The oracle-bone directional example 合集9735 is reported by the CUHK database but the inscription artifact itself was not independently opened and inspected.
The received 詩經 小星 text has an east-direction use, but its exact composition date and earliest physical witness are not established by the inspected pages.

The host/landlord extension is traditionally linked to the host’s eastern seating position; a Tang Du Fu example is reported in dictionary sources, but the first attestation and semantic path are not established here. Listed spring and toilet senses have no verified chronology or semantic bridge here.

For the 東 sound comparison, modern Mandarin dōng and Cantonese dung1 and Baxter–Sagart *tˤoŋ / Zhengzhang *toːŋ are available; the bag/source-word pronunciation is not independently recovered. The proposed loan is not an internal phonetic-component analysis.

The relation between oracle, bronze, Warring States, seal and later forms is documented in categories and broad scholarly summaries, but no complete specimen-by-specimen transition or visual glyph inspection was performed here.

The Shuowen 东 日/木 reading is a historically important account, not proof that 東 originated as a sun/tree compound. NCKU discusses possible cultural and 日/木 interpretations, while CUHK and other modern analyses reject it as a sufficient explanation of the early form.

Modern 东 is widely described by Outlier as derived from a cursive shorthand of 東. The Stockholm dissertation search result mentions Han-period cursive usage, but the PDF could not be opened, so no specific date or specimen path is asserted here.

Xiaoxuetang has a CC0 notice for glyph images obtained via its query interface, but no direct 东 glyph-image URL was exposed in the accessible page text. The selected Commons assets are explicitly modern vector redraws, not ancient artifact photographs.

items.period: Shang-period oracle-bone script tradition; approximate late second millennium BCE script category, not a dated individual specimen
items.caption: A modern redraw of an oracle-script form of 東. The sack interpretation is one scholarly account of the early shape, not a settled identification of its original referent.
items.alt: Black vector outline of an early oracle-script graph identified by the source as 東.
items.selection_reason: Shows the early graphic category discussed in the competing bag and 日/木 accounts; useful with an explicit caveat that this is a redraw and not an artifact photograph.
items.rights: Commons file page declares this representation of ancient script public domain; attribution appreciated. The page traces the illustrated form to source databases and identifies J14291 at hanziyuan.

items.period: Late Shang bronze-script tradition (source page notes 東父乙尊, late Shang); vector image created/uploaded in 2014
items.tradition: Shang bronze inscription tradition, modern vector rendering
items.caption: A modern redraw labelled as a Shang bronze form of 東; the source page links the form to late Shang 東父乙尊. It illustrates a script tradition, not the artifact itself.
items.alt: Black vector outline of a bronze-script graph identified by the source as 東.
items.selection_reason: Pairs an early oracle-style candidate with a bronze-script candidate and gives a source-page attribution to a late Shang object; helps present graph history without pretending the SVG is an artifact photograph.
items.rights: Commons file page declares the vector representation public domain; attribution appreciated. Original inscription image provenance is attributed to listed paleographic databases and sources on the file page.

items.period: Small-seal / Shuowen tradition, transmitted in an Eastern Han dictionary and later editions; modern vector rendering uploaded 2015
items.caption: A modern redraw of 東 in Shuowen seal-script style, associated with the historical 日-in-木 explanation. That account is important in the character’s interpretive history but does not establish the earliest graph origin.
items.alt: Black vector outline of the character 東 identified by the source as Shuowen seal script.
items.selection_reason: Offers a visually contrasting later traditional interpretation alongside the earlier graph candidates, making the difference between a historical explanation and an origin claim teachable.
items.rights: Commons file page declares the vector representation public domain; attribution appreciated. The source page identifies its paleographic databases and hanziyuan image S04417.

limitations.text: All three selected Commons assets are modern digital redrawings of script forms. They are not photographs of oracle bones, bronze vessels, manuscripts or seals, and this researcher did not inspect their pixels.
The file pages identify historical script categories and source records but do not provide a complete palaeographic argument for each glyph’s dating or every transitional step.

The Xiaoxuetang rights notice permits query-interface glyph images and glyph attributes under CC0 1.0, but its accessible entry page did not expose a direct glyph image URL in this inspection. chardb.iis.sinica.edu.tw states All Rights Reserved, so its glyph is not used as an image asset.
